hints: What goes wrong if you start writing zeros the moment you see a 0? Think about how a freshly written zero could fool the rest of your scan.
Split the work into two passes. Pass 1 only records which rows and which columns contain an original zero (two boolean arrays). Pass 2 sets a cell to 0 if its row or its column is marked.

1. Read R, C and the grid.
  2. Make zeroRow[R] and zeroCol[C], all false.
  3. For every cell equal to 0, mark its row and its column.
  4. For every cell, if zeroRow[i] or zeroCol[j], set it to 0.
  5. Print the grid.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Copy the grid; for each original zero, write zeros across its row and column in the copy.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Mark zero rows and zero columns in two boolean arrays, then fill zeros in a second pass.

explain: In the sample the only zero is at row 1, column 1, so zeroRow[1] and zeroCol[1] are marked. In pass 2, every cell in row 1 and every cell in column 1 becomes 0, giving 1 0 1 / 0 0 0 / 1 0 1. Keeping the markers separate from the grid guarantees only original zeros spread. Zeroing during the scan would wrongly turn the whole grid to zeros.
recognize: "For every original zero, clear its row and column" → record first, modify later (two-pass with row/column markers).

import sys
data = sys.stdin.read().split()
pos = 0

def nxt():
    global pos
    pos += 1
    return data[pos - 1]

r = int(nxt()); c = int(nxt())
m = [[int(nxt()) for _ in range(c)] for _ in range(r)]
zr = [any(v == 0 for v in m[i]) for i in range(r)]
zc = [any(m[i][j] == 0 for i in range(r)) for j in range(c)]
for i in range(r):
    print(" ".join("0" if zr[i] or zc[j] else str(m[i][j]) for j in range(c)))
